subject: Career
title: Asking Questions That Impress
description: One-minute skill: Asking Questions That Impress.

hook.text: 'Do you have any questions?' is not a formality. It's the last chance to make an impression.

buildup.text: Generic questions like 'What's the culture like?' waste the moment. They could ask Google that.

discovery.text: Great questions show research: 'I saw you launched X last quarter. How did the team handle Y?'

twist.text: The best question makes the interviewer think. It shifts the dynamic from judge to peer.

climax.text: 'What would success look like in 90 days?' — it shows you're already thinking like an employee.

punchline.text: Your questions reveal what you value. Choose wisely.

quiz.question: What makes a great end-of-interview question?
options: It shows research and forward thinking

details.summary: The questions you ask at the end of an interview reveal your preparation, strategic thinking, and genuine interest. Thoughtful questions shift the dynamic from evaluation to conversation and leave a lasting positive impression.
details.whyItMatters: Interviewers often weight end-of-interview questions heavily because they reveal what the candidate values and how deeply they have researched the opportunity.
takeaways: Prepare five to seven questions and choose the best three in context
Ask about challenges, culture, or strategy rather than logistics
Reference something specific from the conversation in your question

faq.question: What types of questions should you never ask at the end of an interview?
faq.answer: Avoid questions about salary, vacation days, or basic information easily found on the website. Also avoid questions that imply you have already been hired, such as asking about your first project. Save compensation discussions for the offer stage.

faq.question: How many questions should you ask at the end of an interview?
faq.answer: Two to three is the sweet spot. Fewer suggests disinterest; more than four can feel like you are running your own interview. Choose questions that demonstrate insight and genuine curiosity about the role and team.
